newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Key issues unresolved as new EU treaty takes shape.
newsitem.headline: Key issues unresolved as new EU treaty takes shape.

text.p: European Union foreign ministers said on Tuesday they had narrowed their differences over a new treaty to a dozen or so key issues as a deadline looms for agreement in Amsterdam next month.
"There are about 15 points, out of more than 100, that still have to be cleared up," Germany's Klaus Kinkel told reporters at a meeting of EU foreign ministers.

"I can imagine we'll make good progress on these on Friday. There will then remain a few points to be done at Amsterdam," he said, adding a cryptic reference to the likelihood of a "Night of the Long Knives" in the Dutch capital.

EU heads of state and government are due to meet in the Dutch coastal town of Noordwijk on Friday for a half-day informal session to gauge the chances of a successful outcome to an 18-month inter-governmental conference (IGC) treaty review, due to be completed at an Amsterdam summit on June 16-17.

The IGC is designed to prepare for future enlargement that could boost bloc membership beyond two dozen within a decade. It has been overshadowed by the 15-member bloc's ambitious plan to forge a single currency to vie with the dollar and yen on global financial markets,
Although the issues at stake are themselves relatively mundane, the overall package is aimed at creating a more open and efficient bloc.
One EU diplomat said that around 90 percent of a new treaty was in place, leaving the dozen or so most contentious issues to be thrashed out by EU leaders between now and the June summit.

The outstanding issues include the new treaty's centrepiece; the creation by 2002 of an area of freedom and security, lifting all internal borders except those around Britain and Ireland, and taking a firm stand against organised crime, drug trafficking and illegal immigration.

Member countries must also work out how to streamline the bloc's decision-making processes, diluting the national veto with fewer areas requiring unanimity and re-weighting the voting structure in favour of larger EU countries.

Similarly, moves to give a higher profile to job creation and the environment have still to be agreed, as is some form of flexibility to allow some countries to forge ahead and integrate faster than others.
Existing procedures for agreeing common foreign and judicial policies, the key focus for Tuesday's talks, are also expected to be strengthened.

However, there is strong opposition from Britain and the four neutral states -- Ireland, Sweden, Austria and Finland -- to plans to integrate the Western European Union defence arm into the mainstream EU.

While forthcoming elections in France and Ireland lend an air of uncertainty to the Amsterdam talks, the arrival of a more pro-European British government has significantly increased the mood of optimism in Europe.

The demise of the previous Conservative administration, which fiercely opposed many issues favoured by its partners and which had threatened to block the treaty, was widely welcomed as having removed the biggest obstacle to a meaningful agreement in Amsterdam.

New Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair has promised a "fresh start" in Europe. His government has already embraced the social chapter on working conditions and has pledged to cooperate in areas such as human rights and the environment.
